unit-sgt1.title: Test 1 Study Guide · The paper pass
unit-sgt1.source: Study Guide for Test 1, imported as issued

summary.text: The class Study Guide for Test 1, question for question — function transformations (translations, stretches, reflections), intervals of increase and sign, fraction arithmetic, and the percent/ratio review block. This unit is the GRADER for your paper pass: work the printout first, then enter your answers here, untimed. Question numbers match the paper.

why.text: Doing the guide on paper is the real rehearsal — the test is on paper too. Entering your answers here afterward does two things paper can't: it grades you instantly with a walkthrough on every miss, and it quietly files each miss into the Growth Zone so the exact skills you dropped come back for another pass before Test 1.

objectives.text: Write function rules for translations, stretches, compressions and reflections — and go the other way, reading the transformation off the rule.
Find intercepts, intervals of increase/decrease, and where a function is positive or negative.
Add, subtract and multiply fractions and mixed numbers cleanly.
Solve percent and ratio problems, including reverse-percent (part and percent given, whole unknown).

parentNote.text: This is the study guide imported AS ISSUED — Sedona's own idea: paper first, app as grader. All 30 answers were re-derived independently and match the teacher's key. Four questions had to be adapted because their answer choices are graphs the app can't reproduce (19, 26, 28, 29) — each now asks for the equation or rule instead, testing the same skill, and is marked as a study suggestion. The two free-response items (2, the piecewise wage graph; 9, average rates of change) became multiple choice aimed at their key ideas. Workflow: she enters her paper answers untimed; misses go to the Growth Zone automatically. Then tell Claude which numbers she missed — or check the shaky-questions list here — and a Rescue Round of fresh variants on exactly those skills will join this book on her shelf.

nextUp.text: Print or open the paper guide, work it fully, then come back and enter your answers. Enter what you WROTE, not what you wish you wrote — the misses are the valuable part.

cards.def:
**Paper first. App second. Enter what you actually answered.**
• The quiz here is the same 30 questions, same numbers, same letters.
• A miss here is a gift: it gets a walkthrough now and comes back on the review ladder later.
• No clock on this unit — it is a grader, not a race.
cards.hint: The goal of a study guide is finding the holes BEFORE the test does.

cards.def:
**Inside the parentheses moves LEFT/RIGHT (backwards); outside moves UP/DOWN (as written).**
• f(x + 6) is left 6; f(x − 2) is right 2.
• f(x) − 5 is down 5; f(x) + 3 is up 3.
• (x + 5)² − 9 : left 5, down 9 — both at once.
cards.hint: Inside lies, outside tells the truth.

cards.def:
**a·f(x): |a|>1 stretches vertically, |a|<1 compresses, negative a flips over the x-axis.**
• Reflecting f(x) in the x-axis negates the WHOLE rule: x² + 3 becomes −x² − 3.
• A stretch by 7 AND a reflection is a = −7.
cards.hint: Reflection = multiply everything by −1, not just the first term.

cards.def:
**x-intercepts where f(x)=0 (x = ±√c); y-intercept is f(0) = −c.**
• x² − 49: x-intercepts ±7, y-intercept −49.
• Two different questions — don't hand one the other's answer.
cards.hint: x-intercepts: set y to 0. y-intercept: set x to 0. Every time.

cards.def:
**Increasing/decreasing describes the SLOPE; positive/negative describes the HEIGHT.**
• y = −7 − |x| rises until x = 0, falls after — increasing on (−∞, 0).
• g(x) = 5x − 12 is positive where 5x − 12 > 0, i.e. x > 12/5.
cards.hint: Increasing ≠ positive. One is direction, the other is sign.

cards.def:
**Common denominators for ±; multiply straight across for ×; mixed numbers become improper first.**
• 7/8 + 1/6 = 21/24 + 4/24 = 25/24.
• 1/6 · 6¼ = (1/6)(25/4) = 25/24 = 1 1/24.
cards.hint: Mixed numbers are traps in costume. Convert, compute, convert back.

cards.def:
**Translate the sentence: 'is' means =, 'of' means ×, the percent is a decimal.**
• Reverse percent: 1282 is 19% of what? → 1282 = 0.19x → x ≈ 6747.
• Tax: 4% of $56.70 → 0.04 × 56.70 = $2.27.
cards.hint: Say the sentence as an equation before touching numbers.

cards.def:
**A linear function has ONE rate of change everywhere; different rates on different intervals means nonlinear.**
• f(x) = 4 − |x|: rate +1 on [−2,0], −1 on [0,4] — different, so not linear.
• This is the whole point of guide question 9.
cards.hint: Same slope everywhere = line. Anything else = curve or corner.

questions.q: SG #1 — g(x) = 5x − 12. On what intervals is g(x) positive? negative?
questions.hint: Positive means the OUTPUT is above zero. Solve 5x − 12 > 0.
steps: Positive means g(x) > 0: solve 5x − 12 > 0.
A rising line is below zero before its x-intercept and above after: positive on (12/5, ∞), negative on (−∞, 12/5).

ex.main: **Positive on (12/5, ∞), negative on (−∞, 12/5).** The x-intercept 12/5 is the switch; a positive slope means negative-then-positive.
ex.tip: Find the intercept first — sign questions are intercept questions wearing a hat.

questions.q: SG #2 (key idea) — Gordon earns $10/h up to 40 h and $15/h for hours past 40. For n > 40 hours, his weekly earnings E(n) are:
questions.hint: The first 40 hours still pay $10 each — overtime only applies past 40.
steps: Split the week: the first 40 hours pay 10 × 40 = $400, no matter what.
Only the hours BEYOND 40 — that is (n − 40) of them — pay $15.
Total: E(n) = 400 + 15(n − 40), which simplifies to 15n − 200. Piecewise: 10n up to 40, then this.

ex.main: **E(n) = 10(40) + 15(n − 40).** The classic error is 15n — paying overtime rate on ALL hours. The paper answer is a piecewise function; this is its second piece.
ex.tip: Piecewise wage problems: anchor the flat part first, then add the rate × extra hours.

questions.q: SG #3 — f(x) = x². g(x) is f(x) translated LEFT 6 and DOWN 5. The rule for g(x) is:
questions.hint: Inside the parentheses works backwards.
steps: Left 6 goes INSIDE and flips sign: (x + 6)².
Down 5 goes OUTSIDE and keeps its sign: − 5.

ex.main: **(x + 6)² − 5.** Horizontal moves lie (left = +6 inside); vertical moves are honest (down = −5 outside).
ex.tip: Check with the vertex: it should land at (−6, −5). Plug in x = −6 and see the minimum.

questions.q: SG #4 — f(x) = −6x. g(x) is f(x) vertically stretched by 7 AND reflected in the x-axis. The rule is:
questions.hint: Two multiplications: ×7, then ×(−1).
steps: Stretch by 7: multiply the rule by 7 → −42x.
Reflect in the x-axis: multiply by −1 → +42x.
g(x) = 42x. Two negatives (the original −6 and the reflection) cancel.

ex.main: **g(x) = 42x.** Both operations are multipliers on the outside: 7 × (−1) × (−6x) = 42x.
ex.tip: Stack all the outside multipliers into one number before writing the answer.

questions.hint: Common denominator: 24.
steps: LCD of 8 and 6 is 24.
21/24 + 4/24 = 25/24 — just over 1, which fits: 7/8 is nearly 1 already.

ex.main: **25/24.** Sanity check: 7/8 is almost 1, adding more must pass 1 — only 25/24 does.
ex.tip: Estimate before computing; it eliminates half the options for free.

steps: Convert to ninths: 1 8/9 + 3/9.

ex.main: **2 2/9.** Ninths were already on the table — 1/3 just needed the costume change.
ex.tip: When one denominator divides the other, the LCD is the bigger one. No multiplying needed.

questions.hint: Whole parts and fraction parts separately — no borrowing needed here.
steps: Wholes: 8 − 6 = 2.
Together: 2 1/12.

ex.main: **2 1/12.** Since 1/3 > 1/4, no borrowing — the parts subtract cleanly.
ex.tip: Check whether the first fraction is bigger before deciding to borrow.

questions.hint: Mixed number → improper fraction first.

ex.main: **1 1/24.** Multiplying by 1/6 of something slightly over 6 should give slightly over 1 — and it does.
ex.tip: Never multiply a mixed number directly. Improper first, always.

questions.q: SG #9 (key idea) — For f(x) = 4 − |x|, the average rates of change are +1 on [−2,0], −1 on [0,4], and −1/3 on [−2,4]. What do these tell you?
opts: The function is linear, since rates exist on every interval
The function is nonlinear, because the rate of change is not constant
The function has no rate of change at x = 0
questions.hint: What would the three numbers look like for a straight line?
steps: A linear function has the SAME average rate of change over every interval — one slope, everywhere.
Here the three intervals give +1, −1 and −1/3: three different rates.
Different rates on different intervals means the graph is not a single line — f is nonlinear (it is a corner-shaped absolute-value graph).

ex.main: **Nonlinear — the rate changes.** On paper, question 9 wants exactly this sentence plus the three computations shown; the rubric gives full credit for work + conclusion.
ex.tip: On show-your-work items, compute every listed interval, then say what the comparison MEANS in one sentence.

questions.q: SG #10 — Write the equation for this transformation of y = x: a vertical compression by a factor of 1/4.
questions.hint: Compression means the multiplier is between 0 and 1 — and nothing here flips.
steps: A vertical compression by 1/4 multiplies outputs by 1/4.
No reflection is mentioned, so the sign stays positive.

ex.main: **y = (1/4)x.** Compression = fraction multiplier; the negative options sneak in a reflection nobody asked for.
ex.tip: Only apply the transformations named. Extra sign flips are the top distractor trick.

questions.hint: Multiply each OUTPUT by 6; the x values never move.
steps: g multiplies every output by 6: 8→48, 3→18, −1→−6, 7→42, 5→30.
The x column is untouched — vertical transformations never move x.

ex.main: **48, 18, −6, 42, 30.** One clean check: f(0) = −1 must become −6 — any option without −6 at x = 0 dies instantly.
ex.tip: Pick the easiest row (usually x = 0) and eliminate options before computing the rest.

questions.q: SG #12 — f(x) = 3x², g(x) = 9x² − 4. What transformations turn f into g?
questions.hint: How do you get from 3x² to 9x²? And where did the −4 come from?
steps: 3x² becomes 9x² by multiplying by 3 — a vertical stretch by 3.
The − 4 tacked on the end is a translation down 4.
Stretch by 3, then down 4.

ex.main: **Stretch by 3, down 4.** Compare coefficients for the stretch, compare constants for the shift — two separate reads.
ex.tip: 9 = 3 × 3: the stretch factor is new coefficient ÷ old coefficient.

questions.q: SG #13 — f(x) = x², g(x) = (x + 5)² − 9. The graph of g is the graph of f…
questions.hint: Same rule as #3, read in reverse.
steps: (x + 5) inside means LEFT 5 — inside works backwards.
− 9 outside means DOWN 9 — outside is honest.
Left 5, down 9; the vertex moves to (−5, −9).

ex.main: **Left 5, down 9.** Reading transformations off a rule is #3's skill mirrored — both directions are on the test.
ex.tip: The vertex (−h, k) of (x − h)² + k tells the whole story at a glance.

questions.q: SG #14 — What are the x- and y-intercepts of f(x) = x² − 49?
questions.hint: Set y = 0 for one, x = 0 for the other.
steps: x-intercepts: x² − 49 = 0 → x² = 49 → x = ±7.
y-intercept: f(0) = 0 − 49 = −49.

ex.main: **x-intercepts ±7, y-intercept −49.** The trap options mix a correct half with a wrong half — solve both halves before looking at the letters.
ex.tip: Half-right options are ExamView's favorite weapon. Compute fully first, then match.

questions.q: SG #15 — For what values of x is y = −7 − |x| increasing? decreasing?
questions.hint: −|x| is an upside-down V. Where does an upside-down V go uphill?
steps: The −|x| term makes an upside-down V with its peak at x = 0; the −7 only slides it down.
Left of the peak the graph climbs: increasing on (−∞, 0).
Right of the peak it falls: decreasing on (0, ∞).

ex.main: **Increasing on (−∞, 0), decreasing on (0, ∞).** The −7 is a decoy — vertical shifts never change where a graph rises or falls.
ex.tip: Increase/decrease questions ignore vertical shifts entirely. Cross them out.

questions.q: SG #16 — How are y = x and y = x − 5 related?
questions.hint: Subtracting 5 does what to every output?
steps: Every output of x − 5 is exactly 5 LESS than x's output.
Lowering every output by 5 slides the whole graph DOWN 5.
Less, and down — the two halves must agree.

ex.main: **5 less, down 5.** The number story and the picture story are the same fact in two languages.
ex.tip: If your two halves disagree (less but up?), one of them is wrong — recheck.

questions.q: SG #17 — g(x) is the reflection of f(x) = x² + 3 in the x-axis. The rule for g is:
questions.hint: Reflection negates the ENTIRE rule.
steps: Reflecting in the x-axis: g(x) = −f(x).
−(x² + 3) = −x² − 3 — the minus distributes to BOTH terms.

ex.main: **−x² − 3.** The distractor −x² + 3 forgets to flip the +3 — the reflection takes the whole function, constant included.
ex.tip: Wrap the old rule in parentheses, then put the minus outside. Distribute. Done.

questions.q: SG #18 — g(x) is the reflection of f(x) = 3x + 4 in the x-axis. The rule for g is:
questions.hint: Same move as #17, straight line this time.
steps: Distribute: −3x − 4.
Both the slope AND the intercept flip sign.

ex.main: **−3x − 4.** Same rule as #17: everything flips. Two questions in a row means the test cares — expect it Monday.
ex.tip: Repeated skills on a study guide are the teacher underlining what's on the test.

questions.q: SG #19 (adapted — the paper answers are graphs) — y = x − 3 is translated up 2 units. The new equation is:
questions.hint: Up 2 adds 2 to the whole right side.
steps: Translate up 2: add 2 outside → y = (x − 3) + 2.
Simplify: y = x − 1.
On the paper version, pick the graph whose line crosses the y-axis at −1 with slope 1.

ex.main: **y = x − 1.** On paper this is a graph-matching question — find the line crossing y at −1. Here we test the equation behind the right picture.
ex.tip: When answer choices are graphs, compute the new equation first, THEN find its picture.

questions.q: SG #20 — Write 0.036 as a percent.
questions.hint: Decimal → percent: slide the point two places right.
steps: Percent means per hundred: multiply by 100.
3.6% — no rounding involved, so 3.7% is a trap, not an approximation.

ex.main: **3.6%.** Two places right, keep every digit. The 37% option is for point-sliders who go three places.
ex.tip: 0.0__ numbers always convert to single-digit percents. Feel the size before you answer.

questions.q: SG #21 — Marie saved $35, then spent $7 on Wednesday. What is the ratio of her CURRENT savings to her PREVIOUS balance?
questions.hint: Current first. What does she have NOW?
steps: Current savings: 35 − 7 = $28. Previous balance: $35.
Ratio current : previous = 28 : 35.
Divide both by 7 → 4 : 5.

ex.main: **4 : 5.** Order is the whole game — 5 : 4 is the same numbers in the wrong seats, and it is sitting right there waiting.
ex.tip: Underline which quantity the question puts FIRST before forming any ratio.

questions.q: SG #22 — 1,282 people are under age 20, which is 19% of the total population. The total population is about:
questions.hint: The part and the percent are known; the WHOLE is missing.
steps: Translate: 1282 is 19% of x → 1282 = 0.19x.
Sanity: 19% is about a fifth, and 1282 × 5 ≈ 6400 — the answer should sit near there. It does.

ex.main: **≈6,747.** Reverse-percent problems DIVIDE by the rate. Multiplying gives 243 — absurd — and 12,820 is the ×10 decoy.
ex.tip: 'Is' = equals, 'of' = times. Translate the sentence, then solve for whichever letter is missing.

questions.q: SG #23 — What percent of 380 is 190?
questions.hint: 190 is exactly half of 380.

ex.main: **50%.** Spotting that 190 is half of 380 answers it with zero arithmetic.
ex.tip: Scan for halves, quarters and tenths before setting up any equation.

questions.q: SG #24 — Sales tax is 4%. The tax on a $56.70 purchase is:
questions.hint: The question asks for the TAX alone, not the total.
steps: $56.74 is the price-plus-a-typo trap; $22.68 is 40%, a slid decimal.

ex.main: **$2.27.** Each wrong option is a named error: wrong quantity, slid decimal. Read what the question actually asks for.
ex.tip: Tax questions come in two flavors — the tax, or the total. Circle which one before multiplying.

questions.q: SG #25 — A fruit stand charges $3 for 4 pounds. What do 20 pounds cost?
questions.hint: 20 pounds is five 4-pound batches.
steps: Set the proportion: 3/4 = x/20.
Cross-multiply: 4x = 60 → x = 15.
Or spot it: 20 lb = 5 batches of 4 lb, and 5 × $3 = $15.

ex.main: **$15.** The batch shortcut and the proportion agree — two roads, one answer, full confidence.
ex.tip: When the new amount is a clean multiple, count batches instead of cross-multiplying.

questions.q: SG #26 (adapted — the paper shows the graph) — A ride rises from height 0, peaks at 24 m at x = 16 s, and returns to 0 at x = 32 s, in straight lines. Its height equation is:
questions.hint: Up then symmetrically down = an absolute-value vertex form.
steps: Up-then-down in straight lines is an upside-down V: y = a|x − h| + k with vertex (h, k) = (16, 24).
Slope check: it climbs 24 m in 16 s → 24/16 = 3/2, and the V opens downward, so a = −3/2.

ex.main: **y = −(3/2)|x − 16| + 24.** Vertex from the peak, slope from rise-over-run, sign from the opening direction — three reads, no guessing.
ex.tip: On the paper version, pull (h, k) off the graph's peak first; it eliminates most options alone.

questions.q: SG #27 — A function f(x) is shifted LEFT four units. The transformed function is:
questions.hint: Left/right lives inside the parentheses — and lies.
steps: Horizontal shifts go inside the parentheses.
Inside works backwards: LEFT 4 is +4 inside.

ex.main: **f(x + 4).** Pure vocabulary — and the exact rule questions 3, 13 and 28 all lean on.
ex.tip: One mnemonic carries four questions on this guide: inside lies, outside is honest.

questions.q: SG #28 (adapted — the paper answers are graphs) — f(x) is a plane's altitude for a noon departure. The plane leaves TWO HOURS LATE. The new altitude function is:
questions.hint: Everything happens 2 hours later — the graph slides RIGHT.
steps: Leaving late slides the whole timeline right by 2.
A shift RIGHT is minus inside: f(x − 2).
Check with one point: takeoff was at x = 0; now f((2) − 2) = f(0) — takeoff happens at x = 2. ✓

ex.main: **f(x − 2).** 'Later' means right, and right means minus inside — the double-backwards that catches everyone once. On paper, pick the graph slid right.
ex.tip: Test one meaningful moment (takeoff) in the new rule; if it lands at the right time, the sign is right.

questions.q: SG #29 (adapted — the paper answers are graphs) — f(x) = x² + 4, and g is its reflection across the x-axis. Which pair of facts identifies the correct graph?
opts: f opens up from (0, 4); g opens down from (0, −4)
f opens down from (0, 4); g opens up from (0, −4)
f opens up from (0, −4); g opens down from (0, 4)
questions.hint: Reflect the vertex and the direction — both flip.
steps: f(x) = x² + 4 is an upward parabola with vertex (0, 4).
g(x) = −x² − 4: the reflection flips it to open DOWNWARD with vertex (0, −4).
The right picture shows two mirror parabolas that never touch, separated by the x-axis.

ex.main: **Up from (0,4), down from (0,−4).** Reflections flip vertex sign and opening direction together — a graph where only one flipped is the trap.
ex.tip: For graph-choice reflections, check the vertex pair first, the direction pair second.

questions.q: SG #30 — Domain and range of y = |x + 3| − 2, in both notations:
opts: domain: all reals, (−∞, ∞); range: all reals, (−∞, ∞)
questions.hint: You can plug ANY x into an absolute value. The vertex caps the bottom of the range.
steps: Domain: |x + 3| accepts every real number — nothing divides, nothing square-roots. Domain is all reals.
The V's vertex sits at (−3, −2); absolute value opens upward from there.
Outputs start at −2 and go up: range {y | y ≥ −2}, interval [−2, ∞).

ex.main: **Domain all reals; range y ≥ −2.** The −3 belongs to the VERTEX's x-position, not to the domain — that confusion is exactly what options a and b are selling.
ex.tip: Absolute value and polynomial functions always have all-real domains. Range is where the thinking lives.
